name: Building a Claims Tracker
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Receipts: Building a Claims Tracker That Holds Predictions Accountable
lesson.summary: A claims tracker is a simple running log of specific, dated predictions and the claims made to support them, checked later against what actually happened, and it is one of the most effective tools for building an accurate personal sense of which sources and which kinds of claims are worth trusting.
lesson.body:
Most people's sense that a particular field, company, or commentator tends to overpromise is a vague, memory based impression, and that vagueness is a real problem, because human memory is unreliable at tracking base rates over time and is especially bad at remembering specific failed predictions once they have faded from the news cycle. A claims tracker closes exactly that gap. The catalog of broken promises covered earlier in this course is essentially this course's own worked example of a claims tracker, applied retroactively to the quantum computing field. This chapter teaches you to build the same thing going forward, in real time, for any field you care about.

A useful entry stays simple enough to sustain over years, which matters more than making it comprehensive. Record the exact claim in the claimant's own words, not your paraphrase, since paraphrasing tends to accidentally soften or sharpen the original claim without you noticing. Record who made it and what they had to gain from it being believed. Record the specific date and the specific timeframe promised, since a claim that includes a testable date, by 2030, for example, is far more useful to track than a vague one, in the coming years, and the vagueness itself is worth noting as a hype detection red flag the moment it appears. And leave one field blank until it can honestly be filled in later: what actually happened, checked against the originally stated timeframe, not against a goalpost that quietly moved.

The real payoff only shows up after the tracker has been running for a while. Once you have enough entries, you can compute something close to an actual base rate for a specific source or a specific field, for example, of the last ten multi year quantum computing timeline predictions logged from company announcements, how many actually held on schedule. That number, once you have it, is a far better prior for the next claim you encounter than any gut feeling, because it is base rate reasoning and Bayesian updating turned into an actual habit backed by a written record instead of an abstract lesson from earlier in this course.

A few notes on sustaining it in practice. Keep the tracker simple, a spreadsheet with the fields above is enough, no special software required. Review it periodically rather than only when a new claim appears, since a claim that quietly passed its own deadline without anyone checking is exactly the failure mode the catalog of broken promises documents at the level of an entire field. And resist the urge to log only claims you already suspect are wrong, since a tracker that only ever records confirmed skepticism is not actually measuring anything. Log claims you find genuinely plausible too, so the tracker can occasionally prove you wrong, which is what keeps your calibration honest rather than just your suspicion.
